en.title: Big Tech's Dark Side: 3 New Books Expose Corporate Secrets
en.summary: From the inner workings of Big Tech to the psychedelic underworld, August's best-reviewed nonfiction dives deep into compelling narratives. These essential reads offer critical perspectives on modern culture and the pursuit of transcendence.
en.body:
The world of Big Tech is often painted with broad strokes of innovation and progress, but beneath the surface lie complex stories of ambition, exploitation, and the search for meaning. This August, several highly anticipated nonfiction titles have emerged, earning widespread critical acclaim for their unflinching examinations of these themes. Among them, **Claire Stapleton**'s **Don't Be Evil** offers a searing insider's account of corporate culture at Google, detailing a personal transformation from loyal employee to outspoken activist. The book is lauded for its directness, positioning itself alongside other vital critiques of Silicon Valley's impact.

> "A blunt account of one woman’s transformation from eager-to-please corporate striver to clear-eyed activist. It well earns its place alongside other recent accounts of the misdeeds of Big Tech like Sarah Wynn-Williams’ Careless People and Anna Wiener’s Uncanny Valley… Books like Stapleton’s will at least arm people determined to reform them with information they’ll need to make that effort.” –Harvey Freedenberg (BookPage)

Beyond the corporate landscape, **Kimon de Greef**'s **The Ego Trip** takes readers on a wild, often dangerous journey into the world of psychedelic toad venom and the gurus who peddle its promise of transcendence. This investigative work delves into the Seris people's history, the rise of commercial toad milking, and the shadowy competition to develop 5-MeO-DMT into a pharmaceutical. It’s a narrative that explores the fringes of human experience and the often-murky waters where spirituality meets commerce and danger.

## Unpacking the Digital Age and Artificial States

Adding another layer to our understanding of modern complexities, **Jill Lepore**'s **The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State** is recognized as a profoundly important work. In an era increasingly dominated by digital interactions and corporate influence, Lepore’s analysis provides essential context for navigating our out-of-control world. The book is described as staggering and sobering, offering crucial insights for anyone seeking to comprehend the forces shaping contemporary society. Its critical reception highlights the urgent need for such thoughtful examination of our increasingly mediated lives.

## A Soundtrack's Enduring Legacy

While the other titles tackle weighty societal issues, **Ahley Kahn**'s **Days of Miracle and Wonder** offers a deep dive into the creation and impact of **Paul Simon**'s iconic album, **Graceland**. This book is celebrated as a welcome surprise, making readers appreciate the album’s enduring power even more. It’s a testament to how music can transcend its origins, sparking conversations and creating cultural touchstones that resonate for decades. For fans of music and its cultural impact, this is an indispensable read that illuminates the trials and triumphs behind a beloved masterpiece.

## What's Next

These critically acclaimed books are now available, offering readers a chance to engage with some of the most compelling nonfiction narratives of the year. Their reception suggests a strong appetite for in-depth explorations of technology, consciousness, and cultural phenomena, promising continued interest in these subjects from avid readers and curious newcomers alike.

Don’t Be Evil: Bad Bosses, Fake Promises, and My Escape from Big Tech by Claire Stapleton (William Morrow and Company) 4 Rave • 1 Positive • 1 Mixed “A blunt account of one woman’s transformation from eager-to-please corporate striver to clear-eyed activist. It well earns its place alongside other recent accounts of the misdeeds of Big Tech like Sarah Wynn-Williams’ Careless People and Anna Wiener’s Uncanny Valley … Books like Stapleton’s will at least arm people determined to reform them with information they’ll need to make that effort.” –Harvey Freedenberg ( BookPage ) 2. The Ego Trip: Psychedelic Toads, a Trail of Deaths, and the Guru Who Peddled Transcendence by Kimon de Greef (Doubleday) 4 Rave • 1 Positive “A marvelous trip, exploring centuries of the Seris’ tribulations, the growth of commercial toad milking in a region dominated by narco gangsters, quarrels among rival gurus and competition between the sons of an English countess and a German baroness to develop 5-MeO-DMT into a pharmaceutical.” –Annie Bartlett ( BookPage ) 3. The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore (Liveright) 3 Rave • 2 Positive • 1 Mixed “Staggering, sobering, yet essential reading for all who want to understand the arc of this increasingly digital, online, corporate, and out-of-control world.” –Carol Haggas ( Booklist ) 4. Days of Miracle and Wonder: Paul Simon and the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland by Ahley Kahn (Atria) 4 Rave • 1 Mixed “What a welcome surprise … Has only made me appreciate the album’s intricacies and paradoxes all the more … Kahn lets his historical actors speak for themselves as often as possible, collecting a remarkably wide array of voices for so short a book.” –Mark Braude ( The New York Times Book Review ) 5. The People’s Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn by Dave Zirin (Dutton) 2 Rave • 3 Positive • 2 Mixed “Rousing … It’s a wonderful portrait of a historian who reshaped America’s understanding of its potential for change.” –Publishers Weekly
